content: The updated guidance on tuberculosis (TB) treatment will be widely communicated through technical meetings and training activities, ensuring that all stakeholders, including technical partners, are informed. These updates will also be incorporated into a forthcoming revision of the implementation handbook. The 2017 update to the guidelines for treating drug-susceptible TB expands upon the 2010 guidelines by including additional evidence-based recommendations addressing cross-cutting issues relevant to patient care and support for both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB patients. Notably, the 2017 update introduces a decentralized model of care for drug-resistant TB patients, which had not been previously addressed in any WHO TB guidelines. This update is part of WHO’s Global TB Programme’s plan to consolidate all recommendations for managing both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB into a single guideline. The WHO Guidelines Steering Group and the Guideline Development Group (GDG) prioritized questions for the update, focusing on areas of drug-susceptible TB treatment and care that were not addressed in previous guidelines or where new evidence was expected to influence existing recommendations. The scope of the guidelines was limited to specific priority areas, such as retreatment for patients with treatment interruptions or disease recurrence and the effectiveness of decentralized care models for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). Areas without new evidence since the 2010 guidelines were not included in the update, but existing recommendations remain valid and are referenced in the updated guidelines. The primary audience for these guidelines includes policymakers in ministries of health and national TB programme managers responsible for developing country-specific TB treatment guidelines and planning TB treatment programmes. Additionally, healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and educators working in both governmental and non-governmental organizations, are expected to use these guidelines. The recommendations are GRADE-assessed and tailored to meet the diverse needs of health workers and other stakeholders. Separate how-to guidance will be developed later to provide additional implementation details. The guideline development process involved a rigorous evidence review using the GRADE methodology, as stipulated by the WHO Guideline Review Committee. Systematic reviews focused on randomized controlled trials and observational cohort studies, with evidence reviewed and assessed by independent experts. The GDG discussed the evidence and formulated recommendations during a meeting in July 2016, considering the quality of evidence, balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, resource implications, equity, human rights, acceptability, and feasibility. Recommendations were categorized as either strong or conditional based on these factors. The guidelines will be published on the WHO Global TB Programme website and made available in multiple languages, including Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish. They will also be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals to enhance their reach. WHO will work closely with regional and country offices, technical partners, and funding agencies to support the adoption of these recommendations into national TB policies and guidelines. The implementation of the recommendations will be evaluated several years after publication, and the guidelines will be reviewed and updated within 4–5 years or earlier if new evidence emerges.
